narrative:
The model predicted a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors that strongly signaled a higher risk of failure. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the single biggest reason for the negative outcome. Placing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is far below the average of accepted students, who typically rank around the middle of their class. This low ranking strongly pushed the prediction toward failure.

Your LSAT score of 19 was the second most important factor. It sits well below the average of 37 among accepted applicants and pulled the prediction further toward failure.

Third, your first-year class ranking in the lowest decile (again 1 out of 10 versus an average around 6 for accepted students) added more weight in the same direction.

Taken together, these academic performance signals outweighed other details such as your middle-income background and part-time study plans.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Stronger grades and a competitive test score in a future application would likely change the outcome.
